title: "Collectives in a box"– Lebanon
description: Sharing evidence -based learning, tools, templates and approaches from one affiliate across the entire confederation is fully in line and supports the One Oxfam approach. In this context, Oxfam in Lebanon proposes "Collectives in a box" – a "how -to toolkit for establishing and supporting collective structures: Cases of Civil Society Networks, Youth Hubs, and Community Groups".    The concept is built around the notion of "knowledge sharing" and directly speaks to Oxfam Strategic Plan (OSP) operational Goal 2.  This product, which captures four years of experience from Oxfam in Lebanon establishing an array of collective structures, would serve as the go -to reference for the entire confederation. It would act as a practical toolkit to be used and replicated by different Oxfam country programs resulting in effective knowledge sharing and supporting efficiency and simplicity  - the cornerstones of Oxfam's strategic agenda.   Oxfam in Lebanon will demonstrate the importance of taking a systematic, consistent, thorough approach to collectives, walking users through the process step -by -step. Based on Oxfam in Lebanon's experience, applying learning from past collectives can accelerate the successes and achievements of newer ones. The toolkit would provide contextual evidence of Oxfam's return on investment by working with and empowering local actors through unique participatory approaches.  Oxfam in Lebanon has a track record of establishing and facilitating the development of different collective structures, namely Civil Society Organisations (CSOs) networks (e.g. People Affected by the Syrian Crisis (PASC) ; My Work My Right ), and founding platforms/community groups/feminist initiatives (e.g. civic platforms; the Roots Lab initiatives ), a youth hub, and multi -sectoral community peer groups (e.g. Water Sanitation and Hygiene (WaSH) and Protection). description: In the Horn of Africa, East and Central Africa (HECA) region, more than 47 million people were already food insecure due to the triple crisis of floods, locust invasion and now COVID -19.  According to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC)  - November 2021, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is experiencing one of the worst food crises in the world, with 27 million people, or 26% of the population, experiencing high acute food insecurity. The impact of conflict, the primary cause of food insecurity, is long -lasting.  This project will help reduce the impact of humanitarian disasters by more than 8 million people in phase 3+ of acute food insecurity identified in eastern DRC; with a likely increase of 0.21% by the end of the first half of 2022. The strengthening of basic services and other infrastructure (water, hygiene and sanitation, health and education services within the community) must continue to ensure dignified living conditions and equitable access for all communities. Host areas Internally Displaced Persons (PDIs) are often subject to risks and protection incidents due to cohabitation and promiscuity within host families; support for the process of reconciliation between host communities (displacement or return) will be necessary. Mechanisms for prevention and mitigation of protection risks will need to be put in place. Host communities also need access to information on available humanitarian assistance and communication channels need to be adapted to their preferences. In order to prevent tensions and conflict over land between communities. Support for the restoration and development of basic social services and/or essential infrastructure and economic recovery will be considered for returnees.
